name: Victor Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what is a normal day on the line?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the corrugator at a cardboard plant, checking paper moisture, steam pressure and the glue that holds each sheet together. My two-year technical diploma helped me understand the machine drawings, and the crew calls me when the board curls. The lead rate is good and several other box plants are nearby.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is life outside the plant, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Ines and I have no children, and a flat I let out plus savings cover more than six months of costs. I have never used an AI tool; the office can have those screens. I like hearing a clean sheet pass the rollers more than reading a report about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the corrugator crew that a computer can count boxes, but it cannot hear a wet sheet slap the rollers. I would rather fix the glue mix than debate headlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our plant has regular orders, I earn the lead rate, and I own a small flat that I let out. My partner Ines and I have more than six months saved, and there are other box plants within reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep checking steam pressure, glue and paper curl at the start of each run. In a plateau year I would stay on the same shift and leave the AI dashboard to the office, as I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The machine is loud enough without another argument about an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you know the sheet is too wet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It comes off the rollers with a soft slap and begins to bow at the edges. I check the moisture reading, then adjust the heat before the stack grows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new office dashboard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have never used an AI tool and the office handles those reports. If the plant changes my actual controls, I would ask someone to show me, but nothing has changed here.

say: I would tell the **corrugator crew** that wet board still needs a person at the rollers.
I would leave the **AI dashboard** to the office while it stays there.
think: Regular **box orders** and the lead rate make my present job secure.
The **rented flat**, savings and nearby plants protect Ines and me against an ordinary gap.
do: Check **steam pressure and glue** at the start of each board run.
Stay on the **same shift** through the first plateau year.
feel: **Calm**, because the work and household money look steady.
S0.quote: The machine is loud enough without another argument about an app.
fieldNote: Victor listens for **paper moisture** and verifies it with a reading before changing heat.
He has **never used AI** and has no reason to learn an unchanged office dashboard.

steps.text: Keep the corrugator shift and check steam, glue and paper curl

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the canteen that better ordering is fine if the reels arrive on time. I would also say the board has to stay flat, however clever the schedule looks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office planning could get leaner, and a faster schedule might squeeze the minutes between corrugator runs. My own lead post seems safe for now, but I could lose overtime if the plant fills those gaps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would write down paid changeover time for the next four runs and compare the new rota with my payslip. If overtime drops for two months, Ines and I would delay replacing the car; I would keep operating the line while the rate and safety checks hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the possible overtime cut, even with the flat rent coming in. I do not want a screen setting a speed the glue cannot take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changeover cannot be rushed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The glue pan needs cleaning before a different paper grade, or the next board peels at the seam. I would stop the run rather than hide a bad batch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to run the scheduling software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not unless it becomes part of my job, and I would need a paid demonstration at the machine. For now I want the actual rota and pay record, not software lessons.

say: I would accept better **reel ordering** if it keeps paper arriving on time.
I would defend enough **changeover time** to clean the glue pan.
think: My **lead post** may hold, while overtime could shrink under tighter schedules.
Flat rent and **savings** help but do not make a pay cut pleasant.
do: Record **four changeovers** and compare the rota with my payslip.
Delay the **car replacement** if overtime drops for two months.
Keep the **corrugator shift** while paid safety checks remain.
feel: **Anxious** about possible overtime loss and a rushed glue changeover.
S1.quote: I would stop the run rather than hide a bad batch.
fieldNote: He measures the real **pay and timing** effect before changing spending.
The possible **overtime loss** reaches his household even though his base rate and rental income look secure.

steps.text: Delay the car replacement after two months of reduced overtime
Keep running the corrugator while paid safety checks hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI in 2028 could reorder the paper before I start, but a robot that can run this board line comes around 2031. I want to see one handle a warped sheet before anyone cuts a crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be twenty nine at the thinking date and thirty two when capable robots reach the rollers. If the plant loses the lead shifts, the flat rent and savings give us time, but they do not replace my wage for a whole career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the manager for the written staffing plan and keep my current shift while it pays. If two monthly rosters remove lead hours, I would apply to posted nearby corrugator jobs only where base pay matches mine and the safety role is clear; I would not spend savings on an unoffered course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and more than I would admit in the canteen. I know other plants exist, but I cannot assume they will pay the same rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you join a robot trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to watch a supervised paid run on scrap board, with the guard and emergency stop tested. Watching would let me judge the result; I would not touch unfamiliar controls without proper paid instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if no equal-rate job is posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the flat rented and cut the planned holiday before touching the emergency savings. I would stay at the plant if paid shifts and safe work remained.

say: I would ask for a **staffing plan** before robots replace any board crew.
I would want a **scrap-board trial** with guards and an emergency stop tested.
think: At **thirty two**, robots could take lead shifts long before I can retire.
Our **flat rent and savings** buy search time, not a lifetime wage.
do: Keep my **current corrugator shift** while it stays paid and safe.
Apply after **two cut rosters** to posted nearby jobs only at equal base pay and clear safety duties.
Cut the **planned holiday** if no equal-rate opening appears.
feel: **Anxious** about losing lead hours and failing to replace the rate.
S2.quote: I know other plants exist, but I cannot assume they will pay the same rate.
fieldNote: Victor asks to **watch**, rather than claims to learn robot controls or run a trial.
His application needs **two reduced rosters**, an actual nearby posting, equal base pay and clear safety duties.

steps.text: Keep current corrugator shift while paid and safe
Apply after two reduced rosters to posted nearby corrugator jobs with equal base pay, safe duties
Cut planned holiday if no equal-rate opening appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew five years is time to see a real corrugator robot, not a sales film. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and capable hands-on robots around 2034, so the paper reels still need us for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be thirty two when office thinking work changes and thirty five when the physical line is at risk. The good wage, flat and savings help me wait, but I cannot live on them until old age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running the board line and ask the manager for the next contract and staffing figures. If they offer a funded maintenance course with paid workshop days and a posted local job at least at my base rate, I would enrol; after completing it, I would apply for that job only if the safe access duties are written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about having to learn something new, anxious if the shift actually thins. A course in a classroom alone would not teach me to repair a hot roller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which repair would you practise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start with a stopped glue pump under a qualified fitter, with the steam isolated. I want to see the fault and replace a real seal, not click through slides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave for the course before a job appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would require the posted local role, equal base rate, full course funding and paid workshop days first. Then I could take the risk without asking Ines to cover my lost wages.

say: I would ask for **contract and staffing figures** before changing course.
I would want a **real workshop repair**, with steam isolated and a qualified fitter.
think: The **2034 robot date** gives me years of corrugator wages, but no lifetime guarantee.
Our **flat and savings** cannot fund a long career without paid work.
do: Keep the **board line** and request current staffing figures.
Enrol in **funded maintenance training** only with paid workshop days and a posted equal-rate local job.
Apply after **course completion** to that role only with written safe access duties.
feel: **Uneasy** about learning, with anxiety if the shift actually shrinks.
S3.quote: A course in a classroom alone would not teach me to repair a hot roller.
fieldNote: His first choice is **familiar paid work**, but he accepts a practical course under strong conditions.
Training and the later **job application** stay separate and require funding, paid days, a posting, pay and safety terms.

steps.text: Keep running corrugator and request staffing figures
Enrol in funded maintenance course if paid days and posted equal-rate job exist
Apply after completion for posted equal-rate maintenance job with safe access

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the canteen that ten years is a long time, but somebody should keep the machine logs. Thinking AI comes in 2036 and capable hands-on robots around 2039; a forecast is not a machine order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be thirty seven at the thinking date and forty when robots could run the corrugator. I could have another decade of good wages, yet I might waste the warning because I dislike screens and change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the current corrugator shifts and put a new slice of each wage into savings after the rent is paid. In the first year after 2036 I would check the actual board-line staffing and local postings; if the line still pays and stays safe I would work it, and if lead hours end I would seek a posted equal-rate operator role nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. The long wait lets me put the problem down, and I know that is how a surprise catches you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you act before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written plan cutting the lead rota or a safe paid maintenance place with a real job attached. I would not change work because a video claims every factory will be empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the rented flat solve the wage risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Rent from my let flat helps us save, but the tenants also need wages to pay it. I would not count the same money twice.

say: I would tell the crew a **robot forecast** is not a purchase order.
I would keep **machine logs** so actual changes can be checked.
think: At **forty**, I might still need many years of operator wages.
I could **delay too long** because I prefer familiar work.
do: Keep **corrugator shifts** now and add new wages to savings.
Check **staffing and posted jobs** after 2036, then seek equal-rate work if lead hours end.
feel: **Uneasy** because a long warning could tempt me to wait too long.
S4.quote: Rent from my let flat helps us save, but the tenants also need wages to pay it.
fieldNote: Victor treats the **2039 robot date** as a reason to monitor actual staffing, not a certain layoff date.
His added **wage saving** is new money, and his post-2036 job search needs reduced hours and a real equal-rate posting.

steps.text: Keep current corrugator shifts while paid and safe
Add a fresh slice of each wage to household savings
Seek posted equal-rate operator role if lead hours end after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a robot could take my lead shift by 2031 when I am only thirty two. An honest staffing plan, a supervised paid demonstration and posted nearby jobs at my rate would help me decide.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens when a roller starts to sing before the moisture gauge moves. A machine can be measured after the fact, but somebody still has to stop a bad run.

headlineQuote: A machine can be measured after the fact, but somebody still has to stop a bad run.
portrait: **Victor**, 27, leads a cardboard corrugator with a two-year technical diploma and strong practical machine knowledge.
His **lead pay**, rental flat, substantial savings and many nearby plants give him options without guaranteeing equal wages.
He has **never used AI**, prefers familiar work and wants written staffing and safe practical proof before changing jobs.
The fast robot case threatens **lead hours**, while a longer runway permits savings and a conditional maintenance route.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could lead to lost corrugator hours by 2031, early in Victor’s working life.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **staffing plan**, paid supervised demonstration and posted comparable-pay local work would help.
